idiom_name: Drop guard struct (`let _guard = Guard::new(..)`), disarmed by a field or `mem::forget`
implementation_notes: Rust runs destructors when a value goes out of scope - in reverse order of declaration, on early return and while unwinding - so the scope guard is a value whose Drop implementation performs the action: bind it to a name (`let _guard = Guard::new(action);`) and the action runs at scope exit, or hand the value to a closure via a library guard. Commit or rollback variants are modelled by a field the Drop body inspects, or by moving the guard into mem::forget/ManuallyDrop to disarm it; the standard library uses the same shape for MutexGuard and similar types. A hand-written Drop guard is still the right choice when no third-party crate should be added and the action must attach to an already-owned value without allocating.
pitfalls: `let _ = Guard::new(..)` drops the guard immediately (the wildcard moves and destroys it) - bind it to a name such as `_guard` to keep it alive, and note that a moved-from guard is inactive.
A Drop implementation that panics while the thread is already unwinding aborts the process, and panic in a plain drop mangles the original error - the Drop docs tell implementations not to panic.

Partial moves out of a value that implements Drop are rejected and drop-check forbids some self-referential shapes, so a guard that must give its resource back needs Option/ManuallyDrop or the library's into_inner().

variants.name: scopeguard crate macros and value-owning guard
variants.implementation_notes: The crate supplies a guard generic over the value it owns: `scopeguard::guard(file, |f| { let _ = f.sync_all(); })` keeps the value reachable through Deref/DerefMut and passes it to the closure at scope exit, into_inner() recovers it, and the defer!, defer_on_unwind! and defer_on_success! macros declare action-only guards that run always, only during unwinding, or only on normal exit (the scope_exit / scope_fail / scope_success split). Use it when the action must own or recover the resource or when the conditional exit path matters; the hand-written Drop guard remains for dependency-free code and for lock-style wrappers.
pitfalls: The macros expand to a hidden `let` binding: declaring the same guard name twice in one scope shadows the first guard while both still run (in reverse order), and one `defer!` inside a loop body creates one guard per iteration.
`defer_on_unwind!` runs only when the scope is left through a panic and `defer_on_success!` only on the normal path, so picking the wrong one silently drops the action on the other exit.
